title: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether the list reads the same forwards and backwards. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and ideally restore the list afterwards.
shortTitle: Palindrome Linked List — Reverse Second Half, Compare, Then Restore

s1_definition.profdef: Checking a palindrome linked list in constant space is done by finding the middle with a fast and slow pointer, reversing the second half in place, comparing it node by node against the first half, and then reversing the second half back to restore the original structure. This gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space, avoiding the O(n) space of copying values into an array.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank prints a cheque's security code as a chain of digits and wants to confirm it is a mirror code, the same read left-to-right and right-to-left. A clerk finds the middle of the chain, flips the right half around so it points back toward the middle, then walks one finger from the left end and another from the flipped right, comparing digit by digit. Afterwards he flips the right half back so the cheque is unchanged.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the middle, reverse the back half, compare both halves, then reverse back to restore.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checking a palindrome linked list in constant space is done by finding the middle with a fast and slow pointer, reversing the second half in place, comparing it node by node against the first half, and then reversing the second half back to restore the original structure. This gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space, avoiding the O(n) space of copying values into an array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank prints a cheque's security code as a chain of digits and wants to confirm it is a mirror code, the same read left-to-right and right-to-left. A clerk finds the middle of the chain, flips the right half around so it points back toward the middle, then walks one finger from the left end and another from the flipped right, comparing digit by digit. Afterwards he flips the right half back so the cheque is unchanged.

**One line to remember:** Find the middle, reverse the back half, compare both halves, then reverse back to restore.

sections.s2_technical:
A naive approach copies all values into an ArrayList and checks it with two indices from both ends, which is simple but uses O(n) extra space. The in-place approach keeps space at O(1), which matters for very long lists.

Step one is finding the middle using fast and slow pointers. For example, `ListNode slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }`. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. For an odd-length list, slow lands on the exact center, which we can skip during comparison.

Step two is reversing the second half starting at slow. The standard reversal uses three pointers: `ListNode prev = null, curr = slow; while (curr != null) { ListNode next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next; }`. Now prev is the head of the reversed second half.

Step three is comparing. We walk one pointer from the original head and one from prev, comparing values with `left.val == right.val` or, for money, `left.amount.compareTo(right.amount) == 0`. If any pair differs, it is not a palindrome. We only need to walk until the second-half pointer runs out.

Step four, the professional touch, is restoring the list by reversing the second half again so the caller's data structure is unchanged. Many candidates forget this, but mutating an input without restoring it is a side-effect bug that can corrupt shared data in production.

A senior-level nuance is that comparing values rather than node references is essential, since two different nodes can hold equal values. For money, always use BigDecimal compareTo so that 100 and 100.00 are treated as equal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India issues some premium customers a mirror security code on their cheque book, a sequence of amounts that must read identically forwards and backwards as a lightweight integrity check. The system stores this code as a singly linked list and must verify it is a true mirror. This is exactly the palindrome linked list problem.

Problem 2 — The verification runs inside a request on potentially long codes, and we do not want to allocate a whole extra array per check, so we use the O(1) space in-place method with middle-finding and reversal.

Problem 3 — The stored list must come out unchanged because it is the customer's real record, so after comparing we reverse the second half back to its original order.

In the code: a `CodeNode` holds a BigDecimal digit value and a next pointer. A `PalindromeVerifier` has an `isPalindrome` method that finds the middle, reverses, compares, and restores. A `PalindromeDemo` main checks one mirror code and one non-mirror code.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: mirror code 10, 20, 30, 20, 10.

Step 1: Fast and slow both start at the first node 10. We advance slow one and fast two at a time. After the loop, slow rests on the center 30, and slow.next is 20 (the start of the second half).

Step 2: Reverse the second half starting at slow.next. The chain 20 then 10 becomes 10 then 20, with secondHead pointing at 10.

Step 3: Compare. Left starts at head 10, right starts at secondHead 10. Equal. Left moves to 20, right moves to 20. Equal. Right becomes null, loop ends. All pairs matched, so palindrome is true.

Step 4: Restore. We reverse the second half again so the list returns to 10, 20, 30, 20, 10 exactly as it came in.

For the second code 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, step 3 finds 10 versus 50 unequal at the first comparison, so palindrome is false, and we still restore the list.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 21:45:00 [INFO] Verifying first cheque security code (expect mirror=true)
2026-10-26 21:45:00 [INFO] Result 1 -> isMirror=true
2026-10-26 21:45:00 [INFO] Verifying second cheque security code (expect mirror=false)
2026-10-26 21:45:00 [INFO] Result 2 -> isMirror=false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 20 -> 10
    │
    ▼ fast/slow find middle
  slow=30 (center), slow.next=20
    │
    ▼ reverse second half
  first:  10 -> 20 -> 30
  second: 10 -> 20   (reversed from 20 -> 10)
    │
    ▼ compare left vs right
  10==10   20==20   → palindrome = true
    │
    ▼ reverse second half back (restore)
  Output list unchanged: 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 20 -> 10
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Palindrome Linked List ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Two-Pointer (fast/slow) finds the middle                 │
  │  In-place reversal (prev/curr/next) for O(1) space        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: reverse() isolated from compare(); each one job       │
  │  O: compare rule swappable without touching traversal    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │   CodeNode              │
  │  + value: BigDecimal    │
  │  + next: CodeNode       │
  └───────────┬─────────────┘
              │
              ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   PalindromeVerifier                  │
  │  + isPalindrome(head): boolean        │ O(n), O(1)
  │  - reverse(node): CodeNode            │ helper
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. isPalindrome(head)
  2.   find middle (fast/slow)
  3.   secondHead = reverse(slow.next)
  4.   compare head..secondHead node by node
  5.   slow.next = reverse(secondHead)   (restore)
  6.   return palindrome
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a singly linked list is a palindrome in constant space is a four-step in-place technique. First I find the middle using the classic fast and slow pointer pair, where the fast pointer moves two steps for every one step of the slow pointer so that slow lands on the center when fast reaches the end. Second I reverse the second half of the list in place using the three-pointer prev, curr, next reversal. Third I walk one pointer from the original head and one from the reversed second half, comparing values until the shorter side runs out. Fourth, and this is the part many candidates forget, I reverse the second half back so the input list is left exactly as I found it.

The whole thing runs in linear time and uses only constant extra space, which beats the simpler approach of copying every value into an array and checking it with two indices, because that array costs O(n) memory. For a very long list, avoiding that allocation is the whole point.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, premium customers get a mirror security code printed on their cheque book, a sequence of amounts that must read the same forwards and backwards as a lightweight integrity check. I verify it with this in-place algorithm, and crucially I restore the list afterwards because it is the customer's real stored record and leaving it reversed would corrupt the data.

One detail I always stress is comparing values and not node references, because two distinct nodes can hold equal values, and for money I compare using BigDecimal's compareTo so that values like one hundred and one hundred point zero zero are correctly treated as equal rather than relying on equals.
